Aaron Judge playing isn't just about Aaron Judge. It's about making the whole roster work around him.
Judge is most effective in right field, and since he's dealing with a calf strain, that could be problematic if the New York Yankees toss him out there. Whether he plays or not, that leaves Aaron Boone with one of his tougher decisions, and since it feels more likely that Judge won't play unless he can somehow force his way in, right field could get a little messy.
Right field is a major Yankees concern ahead of first playoff series
Lately, Boone's best option in right field has been Heliot Ramos, who's mostly been a bust since the trade deadline, aside from a few moments. For the last two nights, his glove has been an adventure—not in a good way—and it's clear outfield depth is needed right about now.
Unfortunately, there aren't many remedies unless Ramos suddenly turns it around defensively. Based on this week, though, it probably isn't happening.
On Wednesday night, Ramos was late to a ball, and not only did it fall in front of him, but he also bobbled it. This allowed the runner Jonny DeLuca to reach second base on a ball that went all of 202 feet.
Ramos had another gaffe on Thursday night. Taylor Walls was rounding second after a Yandy Diaz single, and when Ramos got to it, he attempted to gun Walls down at third. Instead, the ball sailed on him, went past Amed Rosario, and Walls scored.
Right field at Yankee Stadium isn't the most complex outfield situation. Hence why, when they acquired Juan Soto, who has never been a good outfielder by any defensive metric, they stuck him out there.
If Ramos can't handle it, they have a problem, and since they probably don't want to hinder Judge's calf any more than it already is, they might have to go with somebody out of position.
José Caballero is one name. He has had experience in right field, too.
Last season he had 2 Outs Above Average and 6 Defensive Runs Saved in right in 210.2 innings. This year, he's played just 60.1 innings and has been a neutral defender there, with 0 OAA and 0 DRS. A neutral defender feels like they're sporting Judge's defensive prowess out there, seeing as Ramos has a -4 OAA and -1 DRS in right.
Another name they can go with is Trent Grisham. Grisham, unfortunately, has been compromised due to a hamstring issue, but at this point, he might not have the mobility for center, so right field could be the way to go for him. It's much less ground for him to cover, and if he plays right, that could let Caballero play more of a position of need, like third base.
In this case, it's a matter of who they trust to hit against Boston's lefties more: Ryan McMahon or Grisham, who is fresh off the IL without a rehab assignment. This one, of course, is more outside the box, and the Caballero one feels more likely than Grisham covering right.
That isn't even something Boone has broached in his daily meetings with reporters. At the same time, Caballero has had some outfield experience over the last week, playing center field against the Diamondbacks.
In a perfect world, it would just be Judge out there in right field. Since they're thin on outfielders, and Ramos hasn't been any good out there, they might have to get resourceful defensively as they head into the Wild Card round. These are things you wish the Yankees had figured out earlier, but Boone will have to navigate what's happening.

With the New York Yankees locked into an American League Wild Card berth, anticipation is building around who will make the final postseason roster—especially after former AL Rookie of the Year Luis Gil was optioned to the Florida Complex League ahead of October.
Gil was optioned alongside fellow right-hander Bradley Hanner, leaving one final roster spot up for grabs, as the Yankees announced on Thursday. While Gil had an opportunity to pitch his way onto the October roster, a rocky, walk-heavy outing against the Tampa Bay Rays sealed his fate.
In addition to bullpen decisions, the Yankees are closely monitoring their key injured stars as October approaches. On that front, manager Aaron Boone addressed the media to clear the air regarding conflicting reports about Aaron Judge’s status.
Boone also remains hopeful that slugger Giancarlo Stanton can return in time for the postseason, as the organization continues evaluating his physical readiness through live drills and simulated games.
Luis Gil #81 of the New York Yankees throws a pitch.
Yankees’ potential postseason roster
While the front office awaits definitive health updates on Judge, Stanton, and outfielder Trent Grisham, the baseline roster is coming into focus for their Wild Card showdown against the archrival Boston Red Sox, who are facing injury concerns of their own regarding catcher Willson Contreras.
Here is how the Yankees’ postseason roster is projecting:
- Starting Rotation: Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Carlos Rodón, Cam Schlittler, Will Warren
- Relief Pitchers: David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Michael Fulmer, Brent Headrick, Tim Hill, John Schreiber, Ryan Yarbrough
- Catchers: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez
- Infielders: Jazz Chisholm Jr., Paul Goldschmidt, Ryan McMahon, Anthony Volpe, José Caballero, Luis García Jr., Amed Rosario, George Lombard Jr., Ben Rice (1B/DH)
- Outfielders: Cody Bellinger, Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones
As New York prepares for October baseball, fans are eager to watch the latest chapter in the game’s greatest rivalry unfold, with a spot in the ALDS against the division-champion Tampa Bay Rays hanging in the balance.
Key takeaways
- Luis Gil was optioned to the Florida Complex League ahead of October.
- Aaron Boone addressed conflicting media reports regarding Aaron Judge’s status.
- New York projects Gerrit Cole to lead its postseason starting rotation.

item.content:encoded:
As the New York Yankees try to sort out the final pieces of their playoff plan throughout this relatively meaningless final week of the regular season, there's one position that's quickly gaining interest and intrigue: third base.
Ryan McMahon has gotten the lion's share of reps there over the course of the season, especially after the team began reducing the usage of a struggling Amed Rosario, whose bat and glove seemed to regress heavily in the offseason. José Caballero took over the position during McMahon's brief stint on the injured list, but has mostly ceded it back since.
However, Wednesday night's game notwithstanding, McMahon has struggled mightily offensively, so much so that he might be forcing the Yankees' hand. It doesn't help his case that he's regressed from a Gold Glove-caliber defender to a merely average one.
With McMahon's struggles, the Yankees have opened the door for someone else to take the position in October. While the most likely candidate is Caballero, Aaron Boone revealed Wednesday that an unlikely candidate is emerging: Anthony Volpe.
This could just be to have him ready as a depth option, but it could also be a sign that the team is weighing whether he could give the team the best chance to win at third base. There's reason to believe he can, but also reason to believe it might not be a good idea.
Why Anthony Volpe at third base may work
The simplest reason that it may work is that Volpe is a naturally gifted defender.
In three of his four years in the major leagues, he has graded out positively defensively while playing almost exclusively at the most demanding position, both in terms of range and arm strength.
In 2023, 2024, and 2026 combined, he had 25 Defensive Runs Saved, 21 Outs Above Average, and a 14 Fielding Run Value at the position while playing every day, three marks that were towards the top of the league.
The lone season he was not a good defender was 2025, when he played through a torn labrum for much of the season after an ill-fated dive on his non-throwing arm in May of that year. The immediate bounce-back after he returned from labrum surgery this season is proof that it wasn't spontaneous regression, but rather a fluke.
Still, with George Lombard Jr. grading out even better at shortstop in the minor leagues, Volpe was demoted in early August and asked to try other positions, which he's done since. In 93 innings at second base since being promoted back to the majors, he has 2 DRS and 1 OAA, looking clean and crisp throughout.
But what about third base? Most players who can handle shortstop tend to be even better at second and third base, something that the front office definitely hoped with Volpe after moving him off the position this summer. If he's good at shortstop, how great can he be elsewhere?
His range is undoubtedly his best attribute. Since coming into the league in 2023, Volpe has registered 10 runs of value off his range, which is higher than his actual total FRV of 8. If you remove his compromised 2025 data, he has 15 FRV worth of range value, while his arm and ability to turn double plays are both in the negatives.
So at third base, there's no doubt that Volpe would be very good at knocking down balls and snagging them to his left and right, potentially giving the Yankees a weapon to prevent doubles down the left field line.
But the fact that his arm has been a big negative at shortstop in his career will give some people pause about how good he can be at third base, a position that typically yields a bunch of long throws. That begs the question: does it matter?
Does arm strength matter at third base?
10 years ago, we'd have nothing but our eyes to determine how hard a guy can throw the ball. Fortunately, we have Statcast to help us now.
Volpe's arm strength has consistently been mediocre throughout his career, averaging between 81 and 82 miles per hour on his throws entering this year, when it has undoubtedly dipped due to the sample size at an easier position, per Baseball Savant. That mark consistently sat in the 30th percentile, well below average.
The average speed of a shortstop's throw in the majors is 86.2 mph. The average speed for a third baseman is 84.9 mph. It immediately dispels the belief that a third baseman has to have an equally strong arm, but where would Volpe stack up among those third basemen?
At 81-82 mph, Volpe would comfortably be below average at third base too, sliding in just above Kazuma Okamoto. Of the 53 third basemen with at least 50 throws, Volpe would be 38th.
How are the third basemen in his range defensively? Here are the 2026 defensive stats for the seven players in Volpe's immediate range:
Hao-Yu Lee: -3 DRS, -6 OAA, -4 FRV
Max Muncy (LAD): 3 DRS, 0 OAA, 1 FRV
Kazuma Okamoto: 2 DRS, -3 OAA, -3 FRV
Alex Bregman: 15 DRS, 9 OAA, 7 FRV
Max Muncy (ATH): -11 DRS, -6 OAA, -5 FRV
Brett Baty: 2 DRS, 1 OAA, 1 FRV
Caleb Durbin: 13 DRS, 5 OAA, 5 FRV
As you can see, it's an extreme mixed bag. Bregman and Durbin are two of the best defenders in baseball at their position despite not having a lot of zip on their throws, while Hao-Yu Lee and the Athletics' Max Muncy have been quite bad.
The fact that we have players from all different walks of life here suggests that arm strength doesn't matter nearly as much as some may believe. If a player has good range (the big calling cards of Durbin and Bregman), they can make up for maybe having to bounce a few. If they don't, it becomes a double negative.
It might also help to have a good first baseman at scooping. Paul Goldschmidt is one of the best of his generation at it (and this is now a Statcast stat!), but Luis García Jr. is quite mediocre. That said, the A's Nick Kurtz is significantly better at it than Boston's Willson Contreras and Chicago's Michael Busch.
So maybe arm strength just doesn't matter? If the Yankees deem that it isn't an issue, there should be no reservations about potentially deploying Volpe there come playoff time.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees 6, Angels 3, and for eight and a half innings Wednesday night at Angel Stadium, this one looked like it might stay 1-1 into the parking lot. Cam Schlittler made sure it didn't get out of hand. Austin Wells made sure it never got to an 11th.
Wells' two-out, bases-loaded single in the 10th was the whole game in one swing -- a 1-2 fastball from Luke Murphy that found right field, scoring two and flipping a tossup into a laugher. By the time the inning was over, the Yankees had scored five runs on four straight singles and taken the rubber match of the series, 2-1.
The Turning Point
Extra innings started with Amed Rosario parked on second, the automatic runner, and it took a while to cash him in. José Caballero singled to send him to third. Jazz Chisholm Jr. walked to load the bases. Luis García Jr. popped out for the second out, and for a second it looked like the Yankees might strand the whole mess (they'd left 14 men on base by night's end, which tells you something about how stubborn this offense had been all night).
Then Wells got to Murphy. Two runs scored, Chisholm to third. Cody Bellinger singled him home. Trent Grisham singled Wells home. Ben Rice singled in Bellinger. Four hitters, four singles, five runs, and the Angels never got the third out they needed to escape it.
Star of the Game: Schlittler Rewrites the Record Book
Before any of that happened, Schlittler spent eight innings quietly making history. Two hits. One run. Nine strikeouts. Zero walks. Ninety-nine pitches, 71 of them strikes -- the kind of start where you check the line twice because it doesn't look real for a guy facing a lineup with Mike Trout in it.
That was the 19th time this season Schlittler has allowed a run or fewer in a start. That's a new Yankees single-season record, passing the mark of 18 shared by Ron Guidry's 1978 Cy Young season, Whitey Ford in 1964, and Jack Chesbro all the way back in 1904. Good company. Better yet, Schlittler's still adding to it.
He didn't get the win (no decision, if you're scoring at home), because the Yankees' bats needed extra innings to back him up. He also didn't seem to care. That's usually the sign of the right kind of pitcher.
Detmers Made Him Earn It
Give the Angels' Reid Detmers his due, too. Seven innings, six hits, one earned run, eight strikeouts of his own -- the only damage against him a ground-rule double by Rosario in the fourth that scored Bellinger. For seven innings, this was a legitimate pitchers' duel between two guys who deserved a better final line than "no decision."
Vaughn Grissom's solo homer off Schlittler in the seventh tied it at 1-1 and set up the standoff that lasted until the 10th blew it open.
Boone's Bullpen Math Worked, Barely
David Bednar came in for a scoreless ninth -- one hit, three strikeouts -- and got the win when the Yankees broke through an inning later, which is how it works even if Bednar didn't throw a single pitch in the inning that decided it. Michael Fulmer took the 10th with a five-run lead and made it interesting, giving up a two-run homer to Moisés Ballesteros that scored the Angels' own automatic runner, Wade Meckler. Fulmer got the next two outs anyway. A laugher stayed a win, which is really all that matters in the box score.
Yankees take the series 2-1 after dropping the opener 1-10 on Monday, and they move to 80-60, three and a half back of the Rays with a month to play. San Diego's up next.

item.content:encoded:
The postseason is right around the corner, and the Yankees have more question marks than The Riddler’s suit.
That’s not necessarily a bad thing, at least in some instances, as Aaron Boone revealed that some unexpected players could factor into the team’s postseason plans on Wednesday. While the Bombers don’t expect to have Aaron Judge (right calf strain) when they host the Wild Card series, which begins Sept. 29, Boone didn’t rule out a few faces who haven’t been seen in a while.
“There’s a lot to shake out and unfold over the next four or five days,” the manager said before the Yankees played the division-winning Rays on Wednesday. “Hopefully, we have a lot of options to choose from.”
THE RETURN OF STANTON (AND GRISHAM)?
Giancarlo Stanton, out since April 24 due to three separate calf strains (two right, one left), and Trent Grisham, sidelined by his second right hamstring strain of the season, took live at-bats in Somerset on Wednesday. Both ran the bases, and Boone said Stanton homered while getting six or seven at-bats.
“They’re knocking on the door,” Boone said, but he wasn’t sure if Stanton, a decorated postseason performer, could be ready for the Wild Card round.
The manager previously said that Grisham could be in play, though he wasn’t expected to be activated before the final five games of the regular season.
Asked what he would need to see from Stanton after a five-month layoff, Boone earnestly said, “I’m not sure.”
“I don’t know that answer,” he continued. “Obviously, there’ll be conversations with him. Does he fit on the roster? Is it realistic? All those things, and I can’t answer that right now.”
With the Yankees already log-jammed with first-base/DH types — Stanton can’t play the outfield anymore — Boone added that the former MVP would probably be used as a pinch-hitter, if anything. While not a big role, Stanton’s right-handed bat could be helpful off the bench if the Yankees face the lefty-heavy Red Sox, their likeliest opponent, in the Wild Card round.
Grisham, meanwhile, would give the Yankees an interesting choice in center field with Spencer Jones handling the position in his absence. Jones has outperformed Grisham at the plate, but both are shaky defenders, and the latter has postseason experience that the rookie does not.
LAGRANGE TO DEBUT?
“He’s in the conversation for something,” Boone said of flamethrowing pitching prospect Carlos Lagrange, who threw live batting practice on Wednesday.
But the skipper noted that a lot of “unknown” comes with righty, who has yet to make his major league debut, only recently returned from a shoulder sprain, and has just eight relief appearances under his belt this season. If the Yankees were to use Lagrange and his 100-plus-mph fastball, it would be out of the bullpen.
Asked why the Yankees don’t just promote Lagrange now, Boone said that they still have to cover innings over the last few games of the regular season. They would also have to clear space for him on the 40-man and active rosters.
While Lagrange is 23 and Stanton is 36, both are in similar positions in that they offer the Yankees an intriguing combination of upside, mystery and risk. Asked how Boone might personally weigh all that as the Yankees prepare to make their postseason roster, he said the club will “make the best decision possible” “if those guys are truly pushing into the conversation.”
“Carlos is in the stay ready [phase]. G [got] at-bats today,” Boone said. “All, at least, putting them on the outskirts of the conversation, if nothing else.”
WHO STARTS GAME 1?
Cam Schlittler is the clear frontrunner to win the American League Cy Young Award. So he’s obviously going to start Game 1 of the Wild Card round, right?
“Not necessarily,” Boone said. “We’ll see. Whoever goes Game 1 or Game 2 doesn’t affect the next series. Whoever goes Game 1 or Game 2 can pitch Game 2 and Game 5 in the next series, for example. We’ll decide what makes the most sense, just matching up how we want to go with it. But Cam would certainly be one of those first two games.”
Gerrit Cole, who totaled two earned runs, three walks and eight strikeouts over 5.2 innings and 105 pitches on Wednesday against the Rays, is currently lined up for Game 1 of the Wild Card round on extra rest. The 2023 Cy Young winner, now 22 starts removed from Tommy John surgery, has struggled to get swing-and-miss this season. He’s also faltered against the Red Sox throughout his career. With Max Fried and Carlos Rodón also in the rotation, the case can be made that Cole has been the Yankees’ fourth-best starter lately.
Schlittler, who dominated Boston in last year’s Wild Card series, would be on regular rest if tabbed for Game 1. He is scheduled to make his final start of the regular season on Thursday.
VOLPE AT THIRD? MCMAHON OFF THE ROSTER?
With the lefty-swinging Ryan McMahon putting the finishing touches on an abysmal offensive season and taking a step back defensively, the righty-hitting Anthony Volpe did some pregame work at third base on Wednesday. Boone expects the shortstop turned second baseman to play the hot corner in one or two games before the regular season ends.
“Good to go,” Volpe, who played a few games at third in the minors this year, said of his comfort level at the position.
Meanwhile, José Caballero, another righty, has already gotten some starts at third over McMahon against right-handed pitching. If Volpe shows that he can handle third, it could increase the odds of the Yankees leaving McMahon off their Wild Card roster.
Boone said that he still sees McMahon as a “top-shelf” defender, but he entered Wednesday’s game with -2 Defensive Runs Saved and one Out Above Average, numbers well below career norms. Couple that with a 73 wRC+, and the $16 million man has not been a quality player, though he did hit a grand slam on Wednesday.
“I understand he’s had a couple misplays here along the way, but I want him in the game and the ball hit to him in a big spot,” Boone said. “Offensively, it’s been a struggle, especially in the second half and lately getting it going. But through his struggles that he’s had offensively, he’s gotten a lot of big hits for us, too, along the way.”
On the subject of third base, Boone also said that he hasn’t given much thought to Jazz Chisholm Jr. trying the position again. However, he’s not ruling it out.
WHAT ABOUT OTHER INJURED ARMS?
Fernando Cruz made a rather adamant appearance in the Yankees’ clubhouse on Wednesday. The reliever, out with a partially torn UCL, repeatedly said that he refused to “accept” the diagnosis.
“I had real good inflammation, real stiffness and irritation,” said Cruz, who isn’t considering surgery right now. “People can say it’s a partial tear, but in my heart, it’s not a partial tear.”
While it seems rather improbable that Cruz will pitch again this season, he said that that is his goal, and Boone didn’t rule out the possibility. The righty threw a touch-and-feel bullpen three days ago, and he plans to throw another bullpen on Thursday.
Meanwhile, Clarke Schmidt felt better playing catch on Wednesday than he did on Tuesday after experiencing some biceps cramping over the weekend. However, if the recently returned Tommy John patient is not a viable option by Thursday, “then we’ll probably go a different way,” Boone said, referring to the Yankees’ postseason roster plans.
Finally, Ryan Weathers isn’t expected to throw live batting practice until sometime during the Wild Card series, so he won’t be an option.
With Weathers ruled out and Schmidt’s status uncertain, it will be interesting to see how the Yankees fill out their Wild Card bullpen. On a related note, Boone said that he sees “no scenario” in which the team carries 13 pitchers for the series. They may not even roster 12, he said with so many balls up in the air.
“It depends who’s available and who’s not,” Boone said.

This was the kind of Tuesday that changes the entire shape of a postseason race. The Tampa Bay Rays clinched the American League East, secured a first-round bye, and suddenly made the Yankees’ path look a lot harder than it did 24 hours earlier. For New York, the comfort of having already locked up a postseason berth now comes with a much less comfortable reality: the wild-card round is next.
The Rays finishing on top of the division is not a small footnote. It is the difference between waiting with an advantage and scrambling for survival. Tampa Bay had not won the American League East since 2021, and now it has done it again with the sort of timing that makes the whole thing feel like a statement. The Rays are not just in the playoff picture. They are positioned to matter immediately.
New York got the result, but Tampa Bay got the prize
The Yankees did win Game 1 of the doubleheader, 2-0, behind eight shutout innings from Carlos Rodon, and that should not be ignored. This is still a team that can point to its starting pitching and say, with some justification, that it remains a dangerous opponent in the American League. But that is the problem with baseball’s playoff ladder: one good result does not erase the bigger picture.
Because while New York was grinding through nearly 13 hours at Yankee Stadium, the Rays were doing the one thing that actually mattered most. They beat Max Fried in the nightcap and then walked away as AL East champions. That changes everything. Tampa Bay gets the first-round bye and the cleaner route. New York gets a tougher road and less margin for error.
Jose Caballero summed up the mood perfectly after the clinch. “The 162 first games, it doesn’t matter,” he said. “Now, the clock starts.” That is exactly the point. The regular season can fill the calendar, build the record and create the noise, but once the division is decided, all of that fades. What matters now is who gets the privilege of choosing a better route and who has to fight through the mess.
For the Yankees, the answer is simple enough: they have work to do, and they will have to do it without Aaron Judge for at least the AL wild card series against the Boston Red Sox. That is not a detail. That is a major complication. It leaves New York leaning even more heavily on the very thing that has kept them in the conversation all along: the starting pitching.
So yes, the Yankees can still be taken seriously as a possible team to beat in the American League. But the Rays have made the bigger move, and in October that is often the only move that really counts. Tampa Bay are AL East champions. New York are in the wild-card round. That is the difference between control and uncertainty, and on Tuesday the Rays grabbed all of it.

But Ryan McMahon was back there again against the Rays as the Yankees try to get him right before the playoffs.
And Aaron Boone insisted it’s still possible.
Boone professed his confidence that McMahon remains a viable option, even as the long-slumping player has also regressed on defense.
“Defensively, I have tremendous faith in him moving forward,” Boone said Wednesday. “I understand he’s had a couple misplays here along the way, but I view it as, ‘I want him in the game with the ball hit to him in a big spot.’ ”
That may be the case, but McMahon’s issues with his glove don’t just come down to a few recent errors.
According to FanGraphs, his defensive runs saved have dropped from 10 last season to -2 this year.
And scouts who have watched McMahon have noted a drop-off in his range, glove and overall fielding throughout the season.
“I get why they’re still trying to make it work,’’ one American League scout said. “The other options [at third] aren’t great, especially as you’re staring at the playoffs. But if he’s not going to be not just reliable, but stellar, then the issues with his bat are even worse.”
As Boone noted, “Offensively, it’s been a struggle, especially in the second half.”
Complicating matters are the lefty-swinging McMahon’s issues against left-handed pitching, which could open the door for Caballero or Amed Rosario, especially if they face a Red Sox team that’s filled with southpaws.
Caballero has done well at third but is valued for his ability to come off the bench, while the Yankees have continued to believe that Rosario, who has hit lefties well in recent years, will get back to that after having a hard time against them this season.
McMahon entered Wednesday with a .614 OPS, which ranked 224th out of 232 players with at least 350 plate appearances.
And versus lefties, McMahon has an OPS of .518, also among the lowest in the majors.
That doesn’t figure to lead to too many good matchups for McMahon.
Boone, though, said McMahon has “gotten a lot of big hits for us along the way. Defensively, not much has changed in that I view him as top-shelf over there.”
A year ago against Boston in the wild card, McMahon started just one of the three games, but then had a solid series in the ALDS against Toronto.
“We’ll try to get more out of him offensively,’’ Boone said. “Last year, he went into the postseason and right away had some big hits for us. You never know how that can switch, especially when a guy has the ability like [McMahon] does.”
As for the Volpe experiment, Boone said he wanted to get the converted shortstop over to third “a time or two” before the end of the regular season.
Volpe played three games at third with Triple-A Scranton/Wilkes-Barre this season and would be “ready to go” if called upon.

Cody Bellinger is out of the New York Yankees lineup for Wednesday night's game against the Tampa Bay Rays, but no injury has been reported.
With the top American League wild-card spot secured and Aaron Judge sidelined, the open question is how many at-bats Bellinger takes into a best-of-three series that starts in six days, most likely against the Boston Red Sox.
José Caballero moves into left field against Rays right-hander Mason Englert, according to CBS Sports. The site found nothing pointing to a physical problem and characterized the absence as a pre-playoff day off.
The timing follows a cold stretch. Bellinger opened September by hitting .373 through his first 14 games of the month, then managed just three hits in his next 20 at-bats.
He managed to come through on Tuesday. His fourth-inning, two-run homer off Nick Martinez, his 17th of the season, was the only scoring in a 2-0 Game 1 win before Tampa Bay took the nightcap of a doubleheader 6-1 and clinched the American League East.

Yankees Rest Plan Includes Cody Bellinger
After the doubleheader, manager Aaron Boone singled out Bellinger, catcher Austin Wells and outfielder Spencer Jones as regulars due for rest over the final week, according to Yankees beat writer Gary Phillips.
"As best we can, we'll get ourselves sharp. They're real games, so we're playing, but I definitely will pick some spots to get some guys down. Some of our leverage guys in the 'pen, we want them pitching, but we'll be very selective in how we do it," Boone said as quoted by MLB.com's Bryan Hoch.
Gerrit Cole starts Wednesday, and Cam Schlittler follows Thursday before a three-game series against the Baltimore Orioles closes the schedule, according to Hoch.
At 90-67, New York holds the No. 4 seed and will host the No. 5 seed in the Wild Card Series opening Sept. 29, according to MLB.com. The Boston Red Sox, at 84-73, are the likeliest opponent.
Judge will not be part of it. Boone said the captain has a "moderate" right calf strain and is not expected back for that round, according to Hoch.
"Missing Judge, it hurts. We all know he's the best hitter in the game. For us in here, our mindset is, we're going to have to find a way," Bellinger said, as quoted by Hoch.

Bellinger's September line sits at .338/.351/.581 with five homers and 14 RBI, according to Yardbarker. He has appeared in 76 playoff games, hitting 10 homers and driving in 37 runs.
Bellinger was born July 13, 1995, in Scottsdale, Arizona. The Los Angeles Dodgers drafted him in the fourth round in 2013, straight out of Chandler's Hamilton High School. He won National League Rookie of the Year in 2017 and NL MVP in 2019, when he hit .305 with 47 homers.
His path also runs through a 2020 World Series title with the Dodgers and two seasons with the Chicago Cubs. New York acquired him in a December 2024 trade and, after a 2025 season of 29 homers and 98 RBI, re-signed him in January to a five-year, $162.5 million contract that gives him two opt-out chances and full no-trade protection, according to Bronx Pinstripes.
Limited to 130 games by a 25-game injured-list stint for a left hamstring strain, Bellinger is hitting .268 this season with 17 homers, 73 RBI and 12 stolen bases. His career totals stand at 242 home runs and 768 RBI.

Hours before Wednesday’s meaningless game between the Yankees and Tampa Bay Rays, reporters swarmed Anthony Volpe’s locker as he was seen taking grounders at third base.
Volpe’s locker is positioned next to third baseman Ryan McMahon’s, who sat unnoticed right beside the former top prospect while he was swarmed with questions about potentially playing the hot corner.
It could be a sign of things to come, as the Yankees will be getting the infielder out there at third base — as they did during his time in the minors — at some point during the remaining five games of the regular season.
“I would say it just took a couple, like one session of earlier work, just to get used to it,” said Volpe. “And then I felt like it was pretty comfortable. … t’s definitely more similar to shortstop.”
The Bombers have nothing left to play for as the Rays celebrated winning the AL East on Tuesday at Yankee Stadium and their spot atop the Wild Card standings is locked in.
Therefore, the only value these games provide is trying new things. Volpe at third base is among the most intriguing options.
“Yeah, there’s a lot going on with things from our standpoint being settled as far as our playoff standing and position and everything,” said Boone. “There’s a lot to shake out and unfold over the next four or five days. Hopefully we have a lot of options to choose from, but we won’t know that until Saturday or Sunday and into Monday. …
“I’ll probably get [Volpe] in there a time or two. Just certainly want him working over there a little bit and again trying to be as flexible as possible. There’s a lot of different iterations and ways we can go going into the Wild Card series where if you went heavy position player [on the roster], you could have a lot of options throughout the game and the more position flexibility you have, the better.”
The Bombers’ left-handed heaviness has been well-documented. Boone values balance in the lineup and the Yanks haven’t had much of it.
McMahon has objectively been a weak bat since he’s arrived in New York last season. This season, the 31-year-old is slashing .209/.274/.341 with 10 homers and 35 RBI in 121 games.
Against lefties, it’s even worse.
McMahon is slashing .196/.286/.232 against southpaws this season. That doesn’t bode well entering October, while the book is out on the Yankees’ preference to face righties. Barring some crazy series of events during the final weekend of the regular season, the Yanks will likely be welcoming the Boston Red Sox into Yankee Stadium for a best-of-three Wild Card series.
The Sox are well equipped to potentially go with left-handed starters in all of three of those games. This is where Volpe could potentially come into play.
The 25-year-old has performed respectably since being recalled from Triple-A on Sept. 10. Volpe is slashing .263/.300/.395 with one homer, seven RBI and four stolen bases — reminder, the bar is very low offensively for these Yankees right now.
Against lefties on the whole in his 67 MLB games this season, Volpe owns a .680 OPS — it’s well below average, however, it’s a large improvement from McMahon. The one thing to consider, however, is the potential defensive downgrade to consider with McMahon ranking in the 80th percentile in Outs Above Average at third base.
There is certainly an October role available for Volpe to carve out this season. The third base situation is amongst the many unanswered questions for the Yanks entering the postseason.
McMahon is no shoo-in to make the postseason roster with his season-long struggles at the plate, Jose Caballero hasn’t separated himself — .666 OPS entering Wednesday — although he may be the leader in the clubhouse to get the start at the hot corner.
One could argue that far too many questions remain for the Yankees with the clock winding down this season, however, they hope to have many of them answered over these final few games.

For much of the New York Yankees' 2026 season, there was a constant conversation about who would be the everyday shortstop. The debate surrounded Jose Caballero and Anthony Volpe for most of the year. In the end, the debate over who was better became irrelevant because George Lombard Jr. won the job.
While Caballero is currently without a position, that doesn't mean he doesn't have an opportunity to get everyday reps in the postseason. In fact, maybe the conversation of Caballero vs. Volpe could shift toward him vs. Ryan McMahon. At this point in the season, can the Yankees honestly say McMahon's defense is that much of a difference-maker when he is easily one of the worst everyday bats this organization has ever had?
It isn't hyperbole to mention that McMahon is that bad, either. According to Baseball Reference's Katie Sharp on X, 232 players have over 350 plate appearances this season. He is the only one with an OBP under .280 and a strikeout rate over 29%.
Beyond being a bad hitter, McMahon's defense has regressed. Last season, McMahon had a 7 OAA and 10 DRS. This year, he has a 1 OAA at third and -2 DRS. He can't hit, and apparently his defense — his only calling card as a player — is mediocre at best.
That is why, at this point, it wouldn't hurt to leave McMahon off the Wild Card roster. It isn't a secret that the Boston Red Sox are going to throw an amalgamation of lefties that entire series, and considering McMahon can't hit anybody no matter which side of the mound they're throwing from, Caballero makes the most sense to play every game in that series.
The difference between McMahon and Caballero
That said, Caballero hasn't been all that great this season, either. He has an 86 wRC+ and .666 OPS this year. The one thing he brings is athleticism, and he showed that against the Tampa Bay Rays. In the day game of their day-night doubleheader on Tuesday, Caballero stole second and third with ease.
The Yankees didn't score, unfortunately, but Caballero put them in the position to do so. The Yankees don't get that with McMahon.
Considering McMahon has also regressed defensively, it wouldn't be a downgrade at the hot corner anyway if the Yankees go with Caballero, who has a -1 OAA and 1 DRS at the position. It would just be one bad hitter replacing another, except Caballero is always a threat to steal and brings speed on the bases.
Going from Caballero to McMahon feels like one of the easiest decisions the Yankees have heading into the Wild Card series. At this point, McMahon does nothing better than Caballero, and given that Caballero is already one of the weakest bats in baseball, it's hard to find anything positive about his season.
That said, his ability to put pressure on the opposing teams' pitcher with his base-stealing prowess could be a differencemaker in the playoffs.

Updated Yankees projected Wild Card Series roster without Aaron Judge
NEW YORK - Here was the scenario these Yankees hoped to avoid, but couldn't - a triumphant Tampa Bay Rays team, celebrating their AL East title on Bronx turf.
"They've put together a fantastic regular season to earn that,'' said manager Aaron Boone, after the Rays' 6-1 victory in Tuesday's nightcap of a split doubleheader at Yankee Stadium.
"Hopefully, we get another crack at them.''
That would be in a best-of-five AL Division Series, but only if the Yankees advance from a best-of-three Wild Card series, which they'll host - likely against the rival Red Sox.
With that Wild Card opponent in mind, here is our updated version of a Yankees 26-man playoff roster (12 pitchers, 14 position players), for a series that would begin on Tuesday, Sept. 29.
Rosters can be altered before each postseason round. Injured players can be replaced in-series (pitcher for pitcher, position player for position player) but the injured player is ineligible for the next playoff series.
Projected Yankees pitchers (12)
Starters (3): RHPs Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole; LHP Max Fried.
Relievers (9): RHPs David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Will Warren, Michael Fulmer, John Schreiber; LHPs Ryan Weathers, Tim Hill, Brent Headrick, Carlos Rodon.
On the bubble: RHPs Clarke Schmidt.
Also available: RHPs Luis Gil, Elmer Rodriguez, Yerry de los Santos, Bradley Hanner, Carlos Lagrange; LHP Ryan Yarbrough.
Currently injured: RHPs Fernando Cruz, Angel Chivilli, Kervin Castro.
Analysis: Would the Yanks start anyone but Schlittler in Game 1?
Well, nothing's been firmly stated about the first round rotation, though Schlittler - the odds-on choice for the AL Cy Young Award - would be on normal rest for the opener.
Cole (Wednesday) and Schlittler (Thursday) will make their final regular season starts during this Rays series, though Boone mentioned limiting both starters in these tune-ups for postseason.
In the bullpen, Schmidt's recent bout of biceps cramping wasn't fully resolved as of Tuesday; he was due to be re-examined after a throwing session.
It's possible that even a slight setback takes Schmidt out of consideration for an important playoff spot, moving Michael Fulmer off the bubble and on the roster.
Rodon's eight shutout innings in Tuesday's doubleheader opener was his best effort, during an impressive stretch drive.
He'd be certain to start Game 1 or 2 of a Division Series vs. the Rays, but the Yanks might need his services - in some capacity - to advance vs. Boston, so he's now included here.
Projected Yankees infielders, utility/DH (9)
Infielders (7): Luis Garcia Jr., 1B; Paul Goldschmidt, 1B; Ben Rice, 1B-DH; Jazz Chisholm Jr., 2B; George Lombard Jr., SS; Anthony Volpe, 2B-SS; Ryan McMahon, 3B.
Utility players: (2): Jose Caballero, IF-OF; Amed Rosario, 3B-2B.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: Max Schuemann.
Analysis: Garcia and McMahon are slumping at the wrong time, while Chisholm - who just returned off the IL (right thumb sprain) on Tuesday - has this week to find his rhythm again at the plate.
But that trio of lefty hitters might all be starting on the bench against Boston, which could employ three lefty starters against the Yanks.
That puts Caballero in play as a third base option, with the veteran Goldschmidt (.997 OPS vs. lefties) at first base, the rookie Lombard at short, and Volpe recast as a second baseman.
Projected Yankees outfielders (3)
Cody Bellinger, Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: Jasson Dominguez.
Currently injured: Aaron Judge, Trent Grisham.
Analysis: That's a thin outfield without Judge, whom the Yanks are not planning to have for at least the Wild Card series - per Boone - due to the captain's "moderate'' right calf strain.
It's increasingly unlikely that Grisham (strained hamstring) is available, too, by next week, and that presents a danger considering Ramos' defensive deficiencies.
For that same reason, Dominguez is on the outside. Mostly, the Yanks need the potent right-handed bats of Ramos (who has found his hitting groove) and Rosario to combat Boston's lefty pitching.
Caballero could find himself pressed into outfield duty, too.
Without Judge, "it's going to be super tough on us,'' said Ramos. "But we're going to go forward, for sure.''
Yankees' projected catchers (2)
Austin Wells, Ali Sanchez.
On the bubble: None.
Also available: J.C. Escarra.
Analysis: Wells has been a better offensive presence after a brutal first half, and Sanchez has learned the staff and he earned much praise from Rodon for his contribution to Tuesday's game one win.
Boone has kept the Cole-Wells pairing together, and you'd still anticipate Wells getting starts vs. Boston's lefty starters throughout this opening series.

Chisholm’s most memorable moment, though, was failing to cover first base on a safety squeeze in the 6-1 loss in The Bronx that helped the Rays clinch the division.
With one out and runners on the corners in the seventh inning and Taylor Walls at the plate, manager Aaron Boone said the Yankees were aware that a bunt would be coming “more often than not.”
And sure enough, Walls pushed a bunt toward first base, and Luis García Jr. charged, as he was supposed to, Boone said.
Chisholm started to run over but stopped, believing García would halt his charge and return to the base. Chisholm instead hovered by second base.
“He’s just gotta go [to first base] every time, and he knows that,” Boone said of Chisholm, who acknowledged the mistake.
“Next time, I’ll just keep going through,” said Chisholm, who was sidelined for two weeks after spraining his right thumb Sept. 8 and has returned to a team sorting out its infield with five games to go before the postseason.
Asked before the doubleheader if Volpe would continue to get time at second with Chisholm back, Boone said, “We’ll see.”
Chisholm went 1-for-3 with a single and a walk, while Volpe went 0-for-3 with three strikeouts in the 2-0 doubleheader opener. Entering play, Volpe had hit .286 with a .753 OPS in 10 games with Chisholm on the IL.
The Yankees also have to figure out third base, as Ryan McMahon is a mess on both sides of the ball.
José Caballero got the start there in the opener against Martinez and went 1-for-3 with a pair of stolen bases, with lefty-swinging McMahon in the lineup for the nightcap against Drew Rasmussen. McMahon went 0-for-2 with a strikeout and could not make a difficult play on a Nick Fortes chopper that reached McMahon on an in-between hop and went for an infield single.
Boone said he wanted to get “regular reps” for both Caballero and McMahon, who entered Tuesday just 6-for-40 with an OPS of .402 since returning from a sprained thumb Sept. 1.
Amed Rosario, signed in the offseason with the idea of playing third against lefties, has not produced in those situations this year, and the Yankees have mostly gone with Caballero and McMahon over the last three weeks.
To make room on the roster for Chisholm, Max Schuemann was optioned to the FCL Yankees.
Clarke Schmidt played catch Tuesday after experiencing cramping in his biceps while warming up during Sunday’s game against Arizona.
Boone said the team was awaiting word from doctors regarding the right-hander’s availability, but a source told The Post’s Joel Sherman that Schmidt still felt something in the area.
Another source said an IL stint isn’t out of the question as Schmidt is trying to earn a spot on the postseason roster after missing over a year following Tommy John surgery.
Ryan Weathers threw a bullpen session between games as he works to return from a left forearm strain, and Fernando Cruz (UCL) played catch.
The Yankees haven’t announced their playoff rotation, but Gerrit Cole has started the team’s first postseason game in every season in which he’s been healthy since he joined the organization in 2020.
The right-hander will start Wednesday and was asked by The Post how he would feel if Cam Schlittler got the start in the first game of a wild-card series this season.
“Fine by me,’’ said Cole, who had a similar reaction when there was discussion of having Nestor Cortes open the playoffs in 2022. “What matters is me trying to be my best. Whatever [Boone] thinks is good.”

When Aaron Judge is healthy, he’s the most dangerous hitter in baseball. Sometimes I get alarmed at how uncontroversial a statement that is; ours is a sport that so frequently humiliates those who make such sweeping, unequivocal judgments as those.
But the empirical evidence is what it is. Judge has played 150 or more games in a season four times in his career. In those four seasons, he’s led all position players in WAR four times and led the league in wRC+ three times. He’s been named AL MVP three times and finished second once, ahead of some real doozies: Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer year, Bobby Witt Jr.’s 10.5-WAR campaign in 2024, Shohei Ohtani’s best pitching season — in fact, a healthy Judge is the only thing that’s ever trumped a healthy Ohtani in an MVP race.
So again, it’s not uncontroversial to say that when Judge is healthy he’s the best hitter in the world. He has not, however, always been healthy. Least of all this season, when he missed three months with a broken rib. And now, the single-season AL home run king is back on the IL with a calf strain. The timing could not be worse.
Judge last played on Wednesday, leaving open the option to activate him on Sunday for the final game of the regular season. That seems like a theoretical concern at the moment rather than a practical one. Our Matt Martell was at Yankee manager Aaron Boone’s pregame media availability on Tuesday morning, where Boone illustrated the inadequacy of a return-to-play timeline at this point in the season.
“We’re planning on [Judge] not being a part of [the Wild Card Series],” Boone said. “You hear all the time with injuries, we give ranges: two to four weeks, four to six. They’re ranges for a reason. We’re at a point in the year where, obviously, we’d push it a little bit if that was in play, but that’s a week away. I’m not expecting it, but I’m not ruling it out either.”
That’s the problem. A range of two weeks in recovery time isn’t a big deal in a six-month season, but even one week is twice as long as the Yankees’ entire first playoff round. And muscle injuries can be finicky to begin with — you go to bed one night feeling fine and wake up the next morning with weakness or stiffness.
For what it’s worth, the Yankees are technically still alive in the AL East race as of this writing, but you can forgive Boone for speaking as if the division is already lost.
Either way, in order to speed things along, Judge received a platelet-poor plasma (PPP) injection on Monday, not to be confused with a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection.
Now, apparently having read The Magic School Bus Inside the Human Body as a child is not a sufficient qualification to perform surgery on live patients. At least, that’s what the police told me. But anyone who’s read that book can tell you the makeup of human blood: Red blood cells, which carry oxygen; white blood cells, which fight infection; platelets, which stop bleeding and heal wounds; and plasma, which is the broth all the other stuff floats around in.
PRP injections are a pretty common treatment for sports injuries, but taking the healing bits out of plasma seems kind of counterintuitive. Sort of like a vodka-poor screwdriver. But evidently PPP contains high levels of fibrinogen, which is itself a healing agent. Ms. Frizzle didn’t cover fibrinogen, but sure, I’ll buy it.
Unless the PPP works an actual miracle, though, it looks like the Yankees are going to have to navigate at least the first round of the playoffs without their best player.
And even if Judge does return — either in the Wild Card round or later, if the Yankees advance — I’d caution against assuming that we’d be seeing the best of him right off the proverbial bat. For starters, 99% of star athletes in history are going to try to force their way into the lineup for the playoffs regardless of whether they’re actually healthy.
To say nothing of the fact that Judge can be streaky. This is the nature of Judge’s unusual skill set; there are 1,073 hitters in major league history with at least 5,000 career plate appearances. Judge is the only one of those who’s produced one of the three true outcomes (home run, strikeout, walk) in more than half of his career plate appearances. (I’d like to express my immense gratitude to Adam Dunn, who has a career TTO% of 49.9, for making this fun fact possible.)
Living on the extremes, as he does, Judge will have weeks where he homers every night, and others where he goes 1-for-20 with 12 strikeouts. But you live with it because, over a long enough timeline, it works out heavily in his favor. Among hitters with at least 5,000 career plate appearances, Judge has the third-highest career wRC+, trailing only Babe Ruth and Ted Williams. If you wanted to go further than “best hitter now” and anoint Judge the best hitter ever, leaning heavily on the argument that quality of competition increases over time, you’d have a credible case.
But that’s not what the Yankees got out of Judge this year. In 66 regular-season games, he’s hit .241/.360/.511, with his highest strikeout rate (29.8%) since 2019 and lowest wRC+ (141) since 2020. In seven games since he returned from his rib injury, Judge was just 4-for-23 with one home run, one walk, and 13 strikeouts.
I’ve done enough of these injury reaction posts to figure out that they’re not really about the guy who got hurt, but about the teammates he’s leaving behind.
And I don’t want to underrate the value of Judge — even the version of Judge that has a 141 wRC+, rather than a 200 wRC+ — but the Yankees have done OK without him.
In the weakest American League field in decades, the Yankees are one of only two teams with a winning percentage of .550 or better. Entering their doubleheader with the Rays on Tuesday, the Yankees are still first in the AL in home runs (216) and second in runs scored per game (4.60). Even without Judge (or Giancarlo Stanton, for that matter), their lineup has plenty of beef.

Ben Rice in particular has been absolutely terrific this season. He’s fourth among qualified AL hitters in wRC+ and third in both home runs and runs scored. The Astros have AL MVP frontrunner Yordan Alvarez in their lineup; apart from him, is there any hitter in the AL bracket who’s been Rice’s equal this year? Maybe Junior Caminero? Willson Contreras, if you value OBP over raw power? Even if you’re being charitable, it’s a short list.
Now, past Rice, things get interesting, because if you want to talk about the Yankees’ offensive depth, you have to be able to hold multiple ideas in your head at once.
As of Tuesday morning, the Yankees have 11 hitters with double-digit home runs this season, which is tied for the most in the league. That’s just counting players who have hit 10 or more home runs in pinstripes, and the Yankees brought in substantial reinforcements midseason. Luis García Jr. has just seven homers for the Yankees but 30 overall. Heliot Ramos has four home runs in 32 games and 13 overall, with 20-plus in each of his previous two seasons. George Lombard Jr. has just five home runs in 37 major league games, but he hit 12 dingers in 78 minor league games before he got called up.
Count all this up and the Yankees have more hitters with at least decent pop than they can fit on the roster at once.
At the same time, Rice is the only Yankee with 20 home runs in pinstripes this year. So while this lineup is short on automatic outs, if Judge is out, there’s a massive drop-off after Rice.
If you take Judge out of the picture, Cody Bellinger is second on the Yankees in wRC+, at 119. The Rays don’t have anyone with 100 or more plate appearances and a better wRC+ than Rice this season, but they have four hitters (Caminero, Yandy Díaz, Jonathan Aranda, and Victor Mesa Jr.) with 100 or more plate appearances and a better wRC+ than Bellinger. So do the Rangers (Justin Foscue, Josh Jung, Joc Pederson, Wyatt Langford). The Astros have Alvarez, plus Isaac Paredes and Jeremy Peña. The White Sox have Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami, and Tristan Peters.
As good as Rice has been, the Yankees’ lineup looks concerningly pedestrian without Judge. If you aren’t already a FanGraphs Member, please consider becoming one; it’s the only way to get trenchant original analysis like this.
The good news is that Judge’s calf injury runs counter to the rest of the team’s injury luck. Carlos Rodón, who missed almost three months with an elbow injury earlier this year, dominated the Rays in eight scoreless innings in Game 1 of a doubleheader on Tuesday. The same day, the Yankees activated Chisholm, who’d spent two weeks on the IL with a sprained thumb. Clarke Schmidt just returned from Tommy John surgery last week, and while he suffered biceps cramping in the bullpen on Sunday, it appears to be a minor setback. Trent Grisham remains a question mark for the start of the playoffs as he recovers from a hamstring injury, but his prognosis also looks good.
Judge is as important to the Yankees as any two or three other players put together, but with a healthy and deep rotation and Rice leading the way offensively, they’re not in bad shape. The remainder of this roster could easily survive and advance through a weaker AL bracket, setting the stage for a dramatically timed Judge return in mid-October. Like Kirk Gibson, only bigger.
Michael is a writer at FanGraphs. Previously, he was a staff writer at The Ringer and D1Baseball, and his work has appeared at Grantland, Baseball Prospectus, The Atlantic, ESPN.com, and various ill-remembered Phillies blogs. Follow him on Twitter, if you must, @MichaelBaumann.

And so a strong afternoon effort by the Yankees encouraged and kept their AL East hopes alive, but it more kept those hopes on a ventilator than revive them.
In the first of two games on the day, the Yankees beat the Rays 2-0 in front of an announced crowd of 41,421 in The Bronx during a brisk late-September afternoon that hinted at October.
In all likelihood, also coming soon is the Rays wrapping up the division, but the Yankees (90-66) at least did not allow their rival to celebrate on their grass immediately. Of course, the Rays (95-61) have three more chances to do so, including another that was set for just a few hours later.
“We all believe in each other in this locker room and not looking too far ahead,” said Cody Bellinger, who provided the only run-scoring swing in the victory that clinched no worse than the top wild-card spot.
The Yankees are nearly guaranteed a first-round home date with the Red Sox in a best-of-three series that likely would not include their best player: The club is operating under the belief Aaron Judge will not be available for the series because of his calf strain.
If Aaron Boone’s bunch is going to escape the Red Sox and face off with these same Rays in the ALDS, they would have to rely on their stars rather than their superstar.
On that front, Tuesday afternoon provided some hope with Carlos Rodón (eight shutout, overpowering innings in which he faced just one over the minimum) and Bellinger (a two-run blast in the fourth inning that provided the only runs the club needed) stepping up.
“Just a really solid, quick win,” Boone said of a game that lasted just 2 hours, 2 minutes in large part because of Rodón’s dominance and efficiency, which bodes well for the postseason even if Rodón probably would not get a first-round start.
In his longest, best and likely last outing of the regular season, Rodón struck out eight and allowed just three base runners on three singles.
The first two were erased by double plays (the second, in the sixth inning, entailed Bellinger catching a Richie Palacios line drive and throwing strong to first to double up Victor Mesa Jr.).
The third was a one-out single to Jonathan Aranda in the seventh inning, which might have presented the greatest threat to Rodón. But against Junior Caminero — an MVP candidate who represented the tying run — the veteran reached back for his two hardest pitches of the game (both 97.5 mph fastballs) to get ahead 0-2 before finishing Caminero off with a slider.
“He was awesome. Strike throwing was great,” Boone said of Rodón, who needed 96 pitches to record 24 outs, won his 100th career game and tallied his 1,500th strikeout. “… [He had] velo when he really needed it.”
The Yankees offense was held down by Nick Martinez for three perfect innings before pouncing on two consecutive imperfect pitches to begin the bottom of the fourth.
Ben Rice roped a double down the right field line for the first Yankees hit before Bellinger got a first-pitch sinker across the middle of the plate and clubbed it to right for his 17th homer of the season.
And that was all Rodón needed in a game that might have given the club a blueprint for how it can succeed in October against a team like the Rays and without a monstrous presence like Judge.
“You see the defense today — we’re solid,” said Rodón, who praised José Caballero (a bunt single and two steals in an empty fifth inning) before addressing the rest of the club. “Some lengthy at-bats. Some big-time hits — the homer from Beli there. The bullpen is deep.
“The starters are really good. I have a lot of confidence in this club.”

Los Yankees de Nueva York se impusieron este martes 2-0 ante los Rays de Tampa Bay en el primer encuentro de una doble cartelera disputada en el Yankee Stadium, un duelo que tuvo al pelotero panameño José ‘Chema’ Caballero como uno de los protagonistas de la jornada al desplegar toda su velocidad y picardía en el terreno de juego.
Caballero, quien alineó como titular y se desempeñó en la tercera base, terminó el compromiso de 3-1 con un sencillo y dos bases robadas que mantuvieron bajo presión constante a la batería rival conformada por Nick Martínez y Liam Hicks. En la quinta entrada, el infielder istmeño sorprendió a la defensa con un toque suave que se convirtió en un valioso infield hit, para luego encadenar las estafadas de segunda y tercera base.
Con esta actuación ofensiva, el santeño elevó su total de la campaña a 34 bases robadas en 132 partidos, ubicándose de manera firme en la octava posición entre los máximos estafadores de todas las Grandes Ligas. Su línea ofensiva en lo que va de la temporada se mantiene en .236 de promedio, con 14 cuadrangulares, 51 carreras impulsadas y un OPS de .666.
El triunfo de los ‘Mulos de Manhattan’ también estuvo sustentado en una joya de pitcheo del zurdo Carlos Rodón, quien laboró de manera dominante durante ocho entradas sin permitir anotaciones, tolerando apenas tres imparables y recetando ocho ponches. Con esta labor, Rodón alcanzó su victoria número 100 en las Grandes Ligas y llegó a la cifra de 1,500 ponches en su carrera, en un partido que se completó en apenas dos horas y dos minutos.
La única diferencia en la pizarra llegó en la parte baja del cuarto episodio, cuando Cody Bellinger sacudió un cuadrangular de dos carreras ante los envíos de Nick Martínez para colocar el 2-0 definitivo. The chances are now paper thin after a series loss in Arizona, but if the Yankees are to have any shot of chasing down the Rays in the final week of the season, they absolutely must sweep this four-game series. That required a dominant performance from Carlos Rodón facing one of the AL’s best starters in Nick Martinez. They certainly got that, Rodón running rampant for eight scoreless innings, achieving both the 1,500th strikeout and 100th win of his career as the Yankees took the first game of the day’s doubleheader, 2-0.
Rodón burst out of the gate like he had a point to prove, whiffing the first two batters of the game Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda on a pair of filthy sliders. Cam Schlittler and Max Fried are likely locks for the postseason rotation, meaning if the Yankees elect to stick with a three-man unit, that final spot comes down to Rodón and Gerrit Cole. Aaron Boone has affirmed his commitment to Cole as the Game One starter in a prospective Wild Card Series. This seemingly leaves Rodón on the bubble, which might explain the extra edge he was pitching with this afternoon.
His teammates didn’t do themselves any favors early, burning both ABS challenges in the first inning. I expect the Yankees to tighten the strings on who gets to challenge and in what situation come the playoffs as you cannot deprive yourself of such a vital tool with eight innings still to play.
Martinez entered this game with the lowest walk rate of any qualified starter and among the league’s best at limiting hard contact. He was true to form going the first turn through the order without allowing a base runner. He was helped by the collectively poor approach from the lineup, with four out of the nine batters including the side in the third striking out against a pitcher with the lowest strikeout rate among qualified starters.
That started to change the second turn through the order, the Yankees finally starting to do some damage against the high volume of pitches Martinez was throwing over the heart of the plate, starting with a Ben Rice double into the corner in right to lead off the fourth. The very next pitch Martinez threw rocketed out of the yard, Cody Bellinger blasting a first pitch sinker into the seats in right for a two-run homer — his fifth homer in the last 12 games.
George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones singled with two outs to put runners on the corners. Jones then stole second unopposed, but Anthony Volpe struck out swinging to strand the pair in scoring position. They kept up the pressure in the fifth, José Caballero reaching on a bunt single against his former team and then stealing second and third followed by a Rice walk to put runners on the corners with one out. However, Bellinger popped out and Heliot Ramos flew out as they stranded a pair in consecutive frames.
Rodón settled into an impressive groove after a Chandler Simpson single in the second, retiring the next ten batters in order until Victor Mesa Jr. led off the sixth with a single. After Rodón whiffed Jorge Mateo on a slider for his sixth strikeout, he got Richie Palacios to line out to left. Mesa was running on the play and momentarily forget he had to sprint back to first, allowing Bellinger to throw an absolute seed to Luis García Jr., who applid the tag for the inning-ending double play.
With Rodón’s pitch count standing at just 89 after seven, Boone decided to go batter-to-batter in the eighth. However, Rodón ensured his manager had no choice to make, completing the eighth inning on just seven pitches, including the 1,500th strikeout of his career. It’s tied for his longest start as a Yankee, matching the eight innings he pitched against the Cubs on July 11, 2025.
Rodón entered this start as perhaps the Yankees’ most in-form pitcher behind Schlittler. Including today, in his last eight starts, Rodón has a 1.67 ERA while holding batters to a measly .134 batting average against. He had all his pitches working today, but this really felt like a throwback to his peak years with Chicago and San Francisco. He got whiffs in bunches on the four-seamer above the zone and slider below it. In likely his penultimate start of the regular season, Rodón dominated for eight scoreless innings, allowing three hits and no walks while striking out eight to lower his ERA to 2.67 on the year.
The Yankees didn’t manage another base runner in the final three innings, but Rodón made sure that it wouldn’t come back to haunt them. David Bednar pitched a one-two-three ninth to secure his 35th save of the season. The gap to the Rays now stands at five games as the Yankees become the second team in the AL to 90 wins. At worst, they have clinched the four seed in the AL, guaranteeing home field advantage in a prospective AL Wild Card Series.
The Yankees have a few hours’ rest before taking the field again tonight. Max Fried starts the night game of the doubleheader against Drew Rasmussen. First pitch is scheduled for 7:05 pm ET with the broadcast remaining on YES, so stick around!

Carlos Rodón delivered his best starts of the season Tuesday afternoon, leading the New York Yankees to a 2-0 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in the first game of a doubleheader at Yankee Stadium.
Rodón allowed only three hits, all singles, while striking out eight over eight scoreless innings. It was his first eight-inning performance since July 11, 2025.
The left-hander retired 19 straight batters at one point, with two double plays helping preserve the perfect stretch. Jose Caballero started a 5-4-3 double play in the second inning, while Cody Bellinger caught a line drive in the third before throwing to first base, where Luis García Jr. tagged Victor Mesa Jr. trying to return to the bag.
Rodón also reached a career milestone in the eighth inning when he recorded his 1,500th strikeout. His season earned-run average dropped to 2.67, while he has posted a 1.42 earned-run average in four September starts.
New York’s offense struggled to generate much against Tampa Bay starter Nick Martinez, who retired the Yankees in order the first time through the lineup.
That changed in the fourth inning. Ben Rice opened the frame with a double before Bellinger followed with a two-run home run to right field, giving New York its only runs of the game.
George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones followed with consecutive two-out singles, but Anthony Volpe struck out to end the inning.
David Bednar closed the game with a scoreless ninth for his 35th save.
The victory moved New York to within five games of Tampa Bay in the American League East.
The teams meet again Tuesday at 7:05 p.m. Max Fried starts for New York against Drew Rasmussen.

Yankees utility player Jose Caballero will get the start today at third base in the first game of a doubleheader at Yankee Stadium against the Tampa Bay Rays.
Caballero (age 30) is a former Tampa Bay Ray who was traded to the Yankees at last year's MLB trade deadline. Caballero is hitting a .236 batting average with 14 home runs, 51 RBIs, 32 stolen bases, and a .665 OPS.
Ryan McMahon Yankees Dilemma
This is an interesting development, considering third baseman and left-handed hitter Ryan McMahon has been struggling significantly lately, both offensively and defensively.
This season, McMahon is hitting .208 with 10 home runs, 35 RBIs, and a .618 OPS. McMahon's throws from third base this year have been concerning at times as well. Caballero is an above-average defender and could provide more value offensively than McMahon is right now, so it makes sense why the Yankees are trying Caballero at third base in game one of the doubleheader today against Tampa.
Yankees Getting Ready For Playoffs
With the playoffs (Wild Card) just a week away, with game one beginning Tuesday, September 29th, now is the time for the Yankees to not only rest some key players but also try guys at different positions as they figure out how the postseason roster will ultimately shake out.
The Yankees are also still waiting on the return of Jazz Chisholm Jr., which raises another question: what do the Yankees do when it comes to playing either Anthony Volpe or Jazz Chisholm Jr. at second base, and what happens to the other?
Caballero has talked about trying to provide extra spark/energy to prove himself when playing for his former squad in Tampa. The Yankees will hope to see that effect from a different position in game one of the doubleheader and in this series as they look to wrap up the regular season on a positive note. In contrast, Tampa is looking for a win to clinch the AL East Division, with the winner in a likely wild-card race between the Yankees and Red Sox then going on to face Tampa Bay.
But how Caballero fares today at third base could offer a glimpse into the Yankees' postseason strategy as they prepare for the Wild Card round, which will be no easy task after navigating the AL East. It will also be interesting to see how much this move affects Ryan McMahon's playing time for the rest of the regular season and then the postseason, unless they view it as rest for McMahon.

item.content:encoded:
It felt like Aaron Judge was returning at the perfect time. A September return following a three-month stint on the IL gave Judge enough time to find his timing before the postseason. Unfortunately, Judge suffered another injury before the playoffs even began, hurting his calf in a game against the Minnesota Twins. The New York Yankees hoped it'd be minor, but it was serious enough for the team to place its captain on the Injured List. Now, it sounds as if a return for the Yankees' first postseason series is a long shot at best.
A "moderate grade" calf strain is serious enough for Yankees manager Aaron Boone to proceed as if his best player won't be active at all for the Wild Card series. That is an insanely difficult blow for a Yankees team that, with Judge, is as good as any in a weak American League. For the Yankees to advance to the ALDS and potentially get their captain back, they'll need to rely on this projected lineup below.
What the Yankees lineup could look like without Aaron Judge
Judge is an instrumental piece in the Yankees' lineup for a couple of reasons. First, he's the best hitter in the sport when healthy. That obviously matters. Second, Judge is one of the few right-handed bats on this roster. He provides much-needed balance that, without Judge, the Yankees lack.
| Position | Player |
|---|---|
| Ben Rice | DH |
| Cody Bellinger | LF |
| Heliot Ramos | RF |
| Luis Garcia Jr. | 1B |
| Spencer Jones | CF |
| George Lombard Jr. | SS |
| Jazz Chisholm Jr. | 2B |
| Austin Wells | C |
| Jose Caballero | 3B |
This lineup still has some good pieces in it. Ben Rice has had a breakout year, Cody Bellinger is a well-rounded star, and trails only Yordan Alvarez and Pete Crow-Armstrong, the AL and NL MVP favorites, with a .532 slugging percentage. If Jazz Chisholm Jr. can return from the IL looking like the player he's capable of being, the Yankees can score runs.
The problem, though, is that six of the nine hitters in this lineup are left-handed, and most of them are much better against righties than lefties. The Yankees will use guys like Paul Goldschmidt and Amed Rosario against left-handed pitching, but having Heliot Ramos, who has a .672 OPS since being acquired by the Yankees at the deadline, in the No. 3 hole against righties isn't ideal. The Yankees don't have much of a choice with Judge out, though.
Ultimately, with Judge out, this is a team heavily reliant on lineup platoons. It'll be on Aaron Boone to try to push the right buttons in order to get this offense, which has been remarkably inconsistent without Judge, to score runs against (likely) a potent Boston Red Sox pitching staff.
Aaron Judge injury update: Can the Yankees expect their star to return?
What's most frustrating about the Judge injury update is that we have no idea what the injury is. The Yankees, for whatever reason, keep information regarding injuries, particularly to Judge, extremely close to the vest, making it difficult to know when or even if Judge will be back. All we know is that Judge is dealing with what Aaron Boone deems a "moderate" strain.
That doesn't sound good, especially for a player who has had trouble with the same right calf in the past. In the shortened 2020 season, Judge attempted to return from a calf strain in a couple of weeks, but wound up re-aggravating the injury, pushing his return back several weeks. Calf injuries and other soft-tissue ailments are not to be messed with, and can lead to a major setback if rushed through.
Plus, if the injury was minor, wouldn't the Yankees be quick to tell the world that? I'd love to say Judge is a lock to return at some point, but even if the Yankees were to advance to the ALDS, given how little we know and how tricky returns can be from calf injuries, it's probably wishful thinking to assume he'd be back right at the start of a potential ALDS, which is the last thign any New York fan wants to hear.

The New York Yankees are coming off two straight losses in Arizona to the Diamondbacks, a setback that left them a full six games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League East pennant race.
But the Yankees still have a chance to win the division and with it, the top seed in the AL and a bye out of the Wild card playoff round.
The Yankees and Rays open a four-game, head-to-head series with the first game of a doubleheader Tuesday at Yankee Stadium. With a four-game sweep, the Yankees would take the season tiebreaker and need to win at least two of three against the Baltimore Orioles, while the Rays lose two of three to the Philadelphia Phillies to close out the regular season.
Before Game One of the twin bill, the Yankees announced a decision on how they will utilize veteran first basinal Paul Goldschmidt.
Goldschmidt is out of the New York Yankees lineup for a third straight game, sidelined again by a stark platoon split against right-handed pitching.
The pattern has held all September, and it likely has fans wondering about how much longer the 39-year-old holds even a part-time role with October two weeks away.

Boone's Platoon Explains Goldschmidt Sit
Aaron Boone's lineup card for Tuesday's series opener against Tampa Bay leaves Goldschmidt out again, extending a run that traces back to Saturday. He started Friday against left-hander Eduardo Rodriguez in Arizona and went 1-for-4 with a walk and two runs, then sat both weekend games against right-handers Brandon Pfaadt and Corbin Burnes. That's three benchings in the last three games against right-handed starters.
Why? Goldschmidt has produced an elite 1.006 OPS against lefties this season but an anemic a .572 mark versus right-handers, a gap wide enough that Boone starts Ben Rice at DH and Luis García Jr. at first whenever a right-hander pitches. An Athletic report on the lineup moves after Aaron Judge's calf strain named Goldschmidt and Heliot Ramos as the bats Boone leans on against lefties, with García handling the right-handed side.
Nick Martinez, Tuesday's Tampa Bay starter, has largely dominated Goldschmidt in his career. The former National League MVP is 2-for-10 with four walks and two strikeouts against Martinez, and he is 0-for-13 with four strikeouts in his last three meetings with the right-hander since 2024. Martinez enters at 15-4 with a 2.94 ERA this year, and beat the Yankees in the Bronx in May, giving Boone both the season splits and the head-to-head history pointing toward a Goldschmidt benching.

Goldschmidt's Future in New York
Goldschmidt turns free agent again this winter, and the Yankees have made no public commitment either way. A cheap return as a lefty-masher and clubhouse mentor remains plausible given Rice's grip on first base, and his credentials, a 2022 NL MVP award, seven All-Star selections, four Gold Gloves and five Silver Sluggers still makes him a name teams will inquire about this winter.
First base belongs to Rice, who has grown into an everyday role with 39 home runs and 95 RBI this season, pushing Goldschmidt into a complementary, short-side platoon job. That role fits the final stretch of a one-year, $4 million contract that can grow by $500,000 at each of four plate-appearance thresholds, according to Spotrac, a modest deal compared with the $12.5 million he earned in his first Yankees season a year earlier.
